chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Valuation Matters to You

lessons.title: What Business Valuation Is and Why Founders and Managers Need It

children.text: Three conversations happen in Indian companies every week. A founder in Bengaluru receives a
term sheet
valuing her company at ₹60 crore and cannot tell whether that is generous or insulting. An HR head in Gurugram is told that
ESOP

grants must be priced off a valuation report and wonders why the number jumped 40% since last year. A business head in Mumbai hears the CFO say a competitor was bought at 8 times revenue and nods along. All three are dealing with valuation. None of them needs to become an investment banker. All of them need to know what the number means and where it came from.

markDefs.definition: A short, mostly non-binding document setting out the key terms of a proposed investment: amount, valuation, share class and investor rights.
Employee Stock Option Plan. Employees get the right to buy company shares later at a fixed exercise price.

body.text: A valuation is not a fact you look up. It is a reasoned estimate of what a business is worth on a specific date, for a specific purpose, built on assumptions someone chose. Learn to question the assumptions and you can question the number.

children.text: What Business Valuation Actually Means

Business valuation is the process of estimating the economic worth of a company, a division or a stake in a company. The output is usually a figure or a range, such as "₹240 crore to ₹280 crore for 100% of the
equity

markDefs.definition: The ownership interest of shareholders. Equity value is what belongs to shareholders after lenders are accounted for. Lesson 3.2 separates it from enterprise value.

children.text: Strip away the jargon and every valuation method is trying to answer one question: how much cash will this business put in its owners' hands over its life, and how confident are we of getting it? Cash expected sooner and with more certainty is worth more. Cash expected later, or with more doubt, is worth less.

body.caption: CF is the cash flow in each year and r is the return investors demand for the risk. Chapter 4 builds this step by step.

body.text: You do not need to compute this formula today. Notice its two inputs: cash flows and risk. Every argument about valuation, in a boardroom or across a term sheet, is an argument about one of those two.

children.text: Three Approaches, One Business
In India,
registered valuers
who are ICAI members follow the ICAI Valuation Standards, and Valuation Standard 103 recognises three principal approaches. Almost every method you will hear about sits inside one of them.

markDefs.definition: Individuals or entities registered with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) under the Companies (Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017, to carry out valuations required under the Companies Act, 2013.

cells: Income approach
What cash will this business generate, and what is that worth today?
Discounted cash flow (DCF)
Businesses with reasonably predictable cash flows, such as a mature FMCG or IT services company
Market approach
What are similar businesses worth, or what have buyers recently paid for them?
Comparable company multiples such as P/E and EV/EBITDA, comparable transactions
Sectors with listed peers on NSE and BSE or recent deals
Cost approach
What are the assets worth net of liabilities, or what would it cost to recreate them?
Net asset value, replacement cost
Holding companies, asset-heavy or loss-making businesses, shutdown scenarios

children.text: Worked Example: Three Answers for Kaveri Spices

Kaveri Spices Private Limited is a fictional Coimbatore company selling packaged masalas across South India. Its founder, Lakshmi, is exploring the sale of a minority stake. Here are its FY26 numbers.
Her advisor runs all three approaches.
Cost approach:
net assets are ₹40 crore. This values only the plant, inventory, receivables and cash, after subtracting everything the company owes.
Market approach:
suppose the advisor's set of comparable listed packaged food companies trades at 25 times earnings. 25 × ₹12 crore = ₹300 crore.
Income approach:
a DCF of Kaveri's projected cash flows, discounted at a rate that reflects its risk, gives ₹240 crore.

body.title: Kaveri Spices: equity value under each approach

body.text: Same company, same date, and the answers run from ₹40 crore to ₹300 crore. None of them is wrong. The asset figure ignores Kaveri's brand, distributor network and ability to earn profit. The market figure borrows the mood of listed stocks. The DCF lives or dies on Lakshmi's growth forecasts. A good valuer explains why one approach deserves more weight for this purpose. A good manager asks to see that reasoning.

body.title: Change the peer set
body.prompt: Kaveri's advisor adds two faster-growing listed brands to the peer set, and the peer multiple rises to 30 times earnings. With PAT of ₹12 crore, what equity value does the market approach now give, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 30 × ₹12 crore = ₹360 crore. One change to the peer set moved the value by ₹60 crore. That is why Lesson 3.3 spends a full lesson on choosing comparables.

body.title: Pick the approach
body.question: Deccan Textiles, a fictional company, owns a mill and land in Solapur worth ₹180 crore after paying off all its debts. It has made losses for five straight years with no turnaround in sight. Which approach will a valuer most likely lean on?
options: Income approach, because a DCF is always the most accurate method
Market approach, using the P/E ratios of listed textile companies
Cost approach, because the assets are worth more than the business's earning power
None, because a loss-making company cannot be valued
body.explanation: With no profits, a P/E multiple has nothing to multiply, and a DCF built on continuing losses shows little value. The land and mill are where the value sits. For asset-heavy or persistently loss-making businesses, net asset value often sets the floor.

children.text: Price Is Not Value: What Indian Markets Have Shown
A valuation is an estimate. A price is what someone actually paid on a given day. The two often drift apart, and some of India's best-known companies show how far.

body.title: Two 2021 listings, two very different first days

columns.label: Zomato (now Eternal), July 2021
points: Listed at ₹116, a 52.6% premium to the issue price
Market valued it well above the IPO price on day one

columns.label: Paytm (One 97 Communications), November 2021
points: IPO size about ₹18,300 crore, then among India's largest
Closed its first day about 27% below the issue price
Roughly ₹40,000 crore of investor wealth erased on listing day

children.text: Both issue prices came out of valuation work by bankers. The market disagreed with both, in opposite directions, within hours.

body.title: Byju's valuation as marked by investor BlackRock

body.text: Nobody bought Byju's shares at $1 billion or at zero. These were mark-downs by one investor, BlackRock, re-estimating fair value as delayed accounts, an auditor resignation and a dispute with lenders piled up. A funding round valuation is a snapshot of one day, not a guarantee of anything.

children.text: In Deals, Buyers Pay for the Future
When one company buys another, the price rarely resembles the target's balance sheet. The buyer pays for brands, customers, growth and what it believes it can do with the business.

body.label: HUL's deal for Minimalist (announced January 2025)
body.context: Hindustan Unilever agreed to acquire 90.5% of the skincare brand Minimalist. With FY24 revenue of ₹347 crore, the deal valued it at roughly 8.5 times that year's revenue, a price no net asset calculation would ever reach.

children.text: A year earlier, in January 2024, Tata Consumer Products agreed to buy Capital Foods, owner of Ching's Secret and Smith & Jones, at an enterprise value of ₹5,100 crore. Notice the words "enterprise value". Deal headlines mix enterprise value and equity value freely, and the gap between them can be large. Lesson 3.2 shows you how to tell them apart.
Why This Is Your Problem, Not Just the CFO's

body.caption: Where valuation lands on your desk
headers: The question you should be able to ask

cells: Startup founder
Term sheets, ESOP pools, share issues to angels, an eventual sale
Which method and assumptions justify this number, and is it pre-money or post-money?
Business or product head
Acquisitions, divestments, new business cases, capital budgets
Does this project or acquisition create more value than it costs?
Corporate treasury
Investments in subsidiaries, fundraises, buybacks, impairment testing of acquired businesses
What cash flow forecast and discount rate sit behind this figure?
HR and L&D teams
ESOP grant pricing, perquisite tax on exercise, explaining stock value to employees
Whose valuation report sets the fair market value, and as at what date?
Any employee holding ESOPs
Deciding whether to exercise, tender in a buyback or wait
What is my stake really worth, and when can I actually sell it?

body.title: "Your ESOPs just tripled"
body.scenario: Arjun heads marketing at a Pune-based SaaS startup. At a town hall, the CEO announces a new funding round "at a ₹1,200 crore valuation" and says employee ESOPs are "now worth three times more". Arjun holds 20,000 vested options with an exercise price of ₹100 each. A colleague asks him whether they are all rich now.
body.prompt: What would Arjun need to find out before answering?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Is ₹1,200 crore pre-money or post-money, and how many fully diluted shares does it cover? The price per share, not the headline, decides what an option is worth.
2. What class of shares did the investors buy? Investors usually get preference shares with extra rights, so the round price can overstate what an ordinary share is worth.
3. What fair market value per share does the latest merchant banker's valuation report show? That figure, not the round price, drives the perquisite tax when options are exercised.
4. When can the shares actually be sold? Without a buyback, secondary sale or IPO, the value stays on paper.
5. What does exercising cost? 20,000 options × ₹100 = ₹20 lakh, plus perquisite tax on the gap between fair market value and the exercise price.

body.title: Every valuation has a date, a purpose and a basis

children.text: Before you trust any valuation figure, pin down three things.
Valuation date.
Value can change sharply within months, as Byju's showed. A report dated March 2025 tells you little about September 2026.
Purpose.
A valuation for an ESOP grant, a funding round, a tax filing or a sale can legitimately land on different numbers, because the rules and the users differ.
Basis of value.

ICAI Valuation Standard 102 defines three bases. Fair value is the price between market participants in an orderly transaction. Participant specific value reflects advantages to a particular buyer, such as the synergies HUL expects from Minimalist. Liquidation value is what the assets fetch when the business is shut down.

body.title: The expiry date on a number
body.textWithBlank: A valuation is valid only as at its valuation ___, which is why a two-year-old report cannot price today's ESOP grant.
body.explanation: Every valuation report states a valuation date. Business performance, interest rates and market multiples all move, so the conclusion holds only for that date.

body.title: Before you accept any valuation number
steps: Ask which approach was used, and why it suits this business
Confirm the valuation date and the purpose the report was prepared for
Check whether the figure is enterprise value or equity value
Identify the two or three assumptions that drive most of the number
Find out who prepared it, and whether the law requires a registered valuer or merchant banker for this purpose
Cross-check against at least one other approach

body.label: Screener.in: Hindustan Unilever
body.description: See HUL's market capitalisation, P/E and revenue on one page. In Lesson 3.1 you will use pages like this to pull valuation multiples for listed peers.

cards.definition: A reasoned estimate of the economic worth of a company, division or stake, as at a specific date and for a specific purpose.
Values a business by converting expected future cash flows into a single present value, most commonly through a DCF.
Values a business by comparing it with prices of similar listed companies or recent transactions.
Values a business by its assets net of liabilities, or the cost of recreating those assets.
The date as at which a valuation conclusion applies.
The price that would be received to sell an asset in an orderly transaction between market participants at the valuation date.
Price is what someone paid. Value is an estimate of what the business is worth. They often differ.

points: Valuation is a reasoned estimate built on assumptions, not a fact. Question the assumptions to question the number.
Every method ultimately weighs two things: the cash a business will generate and the risk of getting it.
The three approaches are income (DCF), market (multiples and transactions) and cost (net assets). They can give very different answers for the same company.
Price and value diverge: Zomato listed 52.6% above its issue price, Paytm closed its first day about 27% below, and Byju's went from a $22 billion round to a zero mark.
A valuation only holds for its date, its purpose and its basis of value.
Founders, business heads, treasury and HR teams all make or approve decisions that rest on valuation numbers.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Kaveri Spices, Deccan Textiles and the startup in the scenario are fictional. Figures for real companies are from public reports at the time of the events described. For a valuation used in a transaction, ESOP grant or regulatory filing, engage an appropriately qualified registered valuer or merchant banker.
